“an object is anything that cannot be entirely reduced either to the components of which it is made or to the effects that it has on other things”

Harman, Object-Oriented Ontology: A New Theory of Everything

an object is more than its pieces and less than its effects

the two ways of saying what a thing is

  • “ultimately there are just two ways of telling somebody what a thing is: you can tell them what it is made of, or tell them what it does.” 43
  • “From these considerations it should be clear that there must be some surplus in things that is both deeper than its effects and shallower than its constituent pieces.” 50

every object counts equally

  • “This is the idea that philosophy must begin by casting the widest possible net in aspiring to talk about everything.” 256
  • “The chief enemy of flat ontology is the taxonomical prejudice which assumes in advance that the world must be divided up between a small number of radically different types of entities.” 256
  • “Briefly put, flat ontology is a good starting point for philosophy but a disappointing finish.” 54

objects withdraw from all contact

  • “This withdrawal or withholding of things from direct access is the central principle of OOO.” 7
  • “Fire and cotton are also opaque to each other even if they are not ‘conscious’ in the same way as humans or animals.” 259
  • “Communication between objects is neither easy nor impossible, but both possible and difficult.” 259

two kinds of objects, two kinds of qualities

real objectRO — exists whether or not it currently affects anything else.
sensual objectSO — exists only in relation to some real object.
sensual qualitiesSQ — the qualities a real object meets.
real qualitiesRQ — “These real qualities, too, can only be known by indirect allusion or innuendo.”
the axiomobjects are not identical with their properties, but have a tense relationship with those properties.
  • “In fact, there is always a deep wedge between objects and their qualities, and indeed this principle is the cornerstone of OOO method in every field it has entered.” 91
  • “In combination, these two separate axes of the world (withdrawn/present and objects/qualities) yield a fourfold structure (as shown in Figure 1) that is the basis of the OOO method in every field where it has found relevance.” 259–260

the four tensions

RO–SQspace — “my more general name for the RO–SQ tension is neither ‘aesthetics’ nor ‘tool’, but space.”
SO–SQtime — “This tension can be named time, in the sense of our experience of time rather than that of objective time passing on a clock.”
SO–RQeidos — “the tension called SO–RQ, which we call eidos.”
RO–RQessence — “The name for this tension is essence, since it concerns the real qualities that belong to a real thing.”

the method: how objects meet, and what an encounter produces

metaphor produces a new object

  • “The metaphor that brings cypress together with flame is not knowledge about pre-existing objects, but the production of a new object.” 88–89
  • “Hence the assumption of a ‘vice versa’ at work in metaphor is a fatal error.” 75
  • “This theatrical structure of metaphor strongly suggests that theatre lies at the root of the other arts.” 83

causation is vicarious

  • “Against the assumptions of common sense, objects cannot make direct contact with each other, but require a third term or mediator for such contact to occur.” 12
  • “For OOO, this compositional sense of causation is the primary one, since it holds that any relation between separate things produces a new composite object.” 167

knowledge, and the cost of translation

  • “the claim of OOO is that literal language is always an oversimplification, since it describes things in terms of definite literal properties even though objects are never just bundles of literal properties.” 37–38
  • “There is no translation of anything without energy loss, and hence it is impossible to grasp anything perfectly.” 258
  • “From a OOO perspective, there is no truth: not because nothing is real, but because reality is so real that any attempt to translate it into literal terms is doomed to failure.” 192

aesthetics is the root of philosophy

  • “Aesthetic experience is crucial to OOO as a form of non-literal access to the object.” 260
  • “Thus we can speak of the necessary theatricality of aesthetic experience, despite the art critic Michael Fried’s forceful condemnation of theatre.” 260

the life of an object

  • “When determining the birthpoint of an object, the operative principle should in fact be literalism.” 116
  • “Of the countless relations into which a thing enters during its lifespan, only a small number of them are pivotal, and these are the ones we call symbiotic.” 260
  • “OOO social theory holds that an object is mature as soon as it has no room for further symbiosis.” 120
  • “the phase of decadence begins when an object’s symbioses become overly literal, so that its various attachments become counterproductive to its own survival in a shifting environment.” 121
  • “And all symbioses are asymmetrical in the same way that metaphors are: wine-dark sea is not sea-dark wine.” 260

its rivals

  • “Derrida is a holistic anti-realist who thinks that all language is metaphorical; OOO is an antiholistic realism which views the distinction between the literal and the metaphorical as one of the key oppositions for philosophy and for everything else.” 209
  • “In other words, what Foucault offers is not an object-oriented ontology, but one of its most frequently proposed alternatives: an event-oriented ontology.” 213
Bogost“Bogost employs the term ‘unit’ in much the same way as my own work uses ‘object’.”
Bryant“a theory of six different types of objects: dark objects, bright objects, satellites, dim objects, rogue objects and black holes.”
Morton“a list of five features belonging to hyperobjects: viscosity, nonlocality, temporal undulation, phasing and interobjectivity.”
Bennett“The words in this credo that show Bennett’s ultimate disagreement with OOO are ‘one’, ‘matter’, and ‘doing things’.”
Garcia“For Garcia, things are always outside themselves in the world.”

a poetics of a thing

the principles, in the book's own terms

  1. “All objects must be given equal attention, whether they be human, nonhuman, natural, cultural, real or fictional.”
  2. “Objects are not identical with their properties, but have a tense relationship with those properties, and this very tension is responsible for all of the change that occurs in the world.”
  3. “Objects come in just two kinds: real objects exist whether or not they currently affect anything else, while sensual objects exist only in relation to some real object.”
  4. “Real objects cannot relate to one another directly, but only indirectly, by means of a sensual object.”
  5. “The properties of objects also come in just two kinds: again, real and sensual.”
  6. “These two kinds of objects and two kinds of qualities lead to four basic permutations, which OOO treats as the root of time and space, as well as two closely related terms known as essence and eidos.”
  7. “Finally, OOO holds that philosophy generally has a closer relationship with aesthetics than with mathematics or natural science.”
